lessons.title: Format Converter: pré-visualizar e converter arquivos de imagem
lessons.description: Selecione uma pasta de origem, confira os nomes de destino e as atribuições de canais, converta as imagens e retome o trabalho já concluído.
objectives: Escolher as pastas de origem e de destino com o layout de aquisição correto.
Pré-visualizar os nomes de destino, os campos e as atribuições de canais.
Converter os arquivos e usar Resume para os campos já concluídos.
lessons.prerequisite: Prepare uma pasta de arquivos de imagem compatíveis e preserve os metadados de aquisição deles. Você pode praticar com as duas imagens TIFF do tutorial de Import Project. Defina o layout e o tratamento de Z de acordo com a sua aquisição.

objectives: Associar imagens, máscaras e linhas de medições.

Importar o projeto e inspecionar as saídas.

lessons.title: Batch Runner: configurar e executar uma fila

objectives: Adicionar trabalhos com suas configurações e dependências.
Salvar, executar e continuar a fila.
Inspecionar o registro e as saídas de cada trabalho.

scenes.narration: Use os controles de movimentação para ordenar os trabalhos. Uma dependência precisa aparecer antes do trabalho que depende dela; leia as mensagens de validação e corrija a ordem.

lessons.title: Classify: escolher um modelo e explorar os resultados
lessons.description: Escolha a classificação por imagens ou por características, carregue dados de exemplo, inspecione os resultados de previsão e abra as ferramentas relacionadas dentro do Classify.
objectives: Escolher Computer Vision para imagens ou Tabular Machine Learning para medições.
Começar com dados de teste e seguir o passo a passo de treinamento correspondente.
Inspecionar as previsões e abrir as ferramentas de avaliação, de características e de treinamento.
lessons.prerequisite: Abra o Classify na tela Home. Use Load test data para um projeto de exemplo. Para o seu próprio projeto, prepare recortes de objetos ou características medidas e rótulos de classe vindos de anotações ou de metadados experimentais.

scenes.narration: Abra o Classify na tela Home. Comece escolhendo a família de classificadores. As aulas de imagens e de dados tabulares indicadas aqui mostram, cada uma, um exemplo completo.
scenes.speech_text: Abra o Classify na tela Home. Comece escolhendo a família de classificadores. As aulas de imagens e de dados tabulares indicadas aqui mostram, cada uma, um exemplo completo.

scenes.narration: Escolha Computer Vision para aprender com imagens de objetos. Escolha Tabular Machine Learning para aprender com colunas de características medidas. O Measure fornece essas entradas, e o Annotate permite adicionar rótulos aos objetos.

scenes.narration: No exemplo tabular, clique em Load test data e escolha Load. Selecione os rótulos de classe e as configurações de características e siga a aula tabular para treinar o modelo e salvar as previsões.

scenes.narration: Depois da execução tabular, inspecione o mapa de calor das previsões e as pontuações salvas por objeto. Objetos sem as medições necessárias podem ficar sem pontuação. lessons.title: Curate: editar máscaras e trajetórias

objectives: Editar uma máscara de rótulos com o pincel e os controles de desfazer.
Dividir, unir e salvar trajetórias.
Preservar os arquivos de origem e o histórico de curadoria.

scenes.narration: Abra Make Masks e depois Curate para editar máscaras de rótulos e trajetórias. Baixe o exemplo de prática sintético abaixo e guarde uma cópia intacta.

lessons.title: Illumination: estimar e inspecionar um modelo de correção
lessons.description: Escolha os canais de imagem, estime um campo de iluminação, inspecione a figura de controle de qualidade e reutilize o modelo salvo.
objectives: Selecionar campos representativos e canais de intensidade.
Estimar e inspecionar um modelo de iluminação.
Reutilizar o modelo no Mask ou no Measure.
lessons.prerequisite: Use uma pasta de imagens combinadas com campos representativos de cada grupo de aquisição. O exemplo usa os dezesseis campos do exemplo de placa baixado no Measure. Saiba quais planos salvos contêm intensidades e quais contêm rótulos.

scenes.narration: Abra o Measure e depois Illumination para estimar um modelo de correção do brilho irregular das imagens.
scenes.speech_text: Abra o Measure e depois Illumination para estimar um modelo de correção do brilho irregular das imagens.

scenes.narration: Defina Source como a pasta merged que contém os arranjos de imagem. Use campos representativos da sua aquisição; o exemplo usa dezesseis campos de uma placa.
scenes.speech_text: Defina Source como a pasta merged que contém os arranjos de imagem. Use campos representativos da sua aquisição; o exemplo usa dezesseis campos de uma placa.

scenes.narration: Defina Channels como os planos de intensidade salvos que você quer corrigir. O exemplo usa o canal zero. Confira o mapeamento de canais e exclua os planos de máscaras de rótulos.
scenes.speech_text: Defina Channels como os planos de intensidade salvos que você quer corrigir. O exemplo usa o canal zero. Confira o mapeamento de canais e exclua os planos de máscaras de rótulos.

scenes.narration: Ative Illumination correction antes de estimar um campo. Se estiver desativado, o Run termina sem criar um modelo de correção.
scenes.speech_text: Ative Illumination correction antes de estimar um campo. Se estiver desativado, o Run termina sem criar um modelo de correção.

scenes.narration: Escolha um estimador e as configurações dele. No exemplo polinomial, use grau quatro e deixe Illumination model vazio para estimar um campo novo. Procure no resultado estruturas que pertencem às células e não à iluminação.
scenes.speech_text: Escolha um estimador e as configurações dele. No exemplo polinomial, use grau quatro e deixe Illumination model vazio para estimar um campo novo. Procure no resultado estruturas que pertencem às células e não à iluminação.

scenes.narration: Ative Illumination per plate para ajustar grupos de aquisição separadamente. Defina Maximum fields como uma amostra representativa; o exemplo inclui os dezesseis campos disponíveis.
scenes.speech_text: Ative Illumination per plate para ajustar grupos de aquisição separadamente. Defina Maximum fields como uma amostra representativa; o exemplo inclui os dezesseis campos disponíveis.

scenes.narration: Defina Illumination dark a partir da calibração da sua câmera, quando houver. É um deslocamento aditivo em contagens brutas; zero é o valor do exemplo.
scenes.speech_text: Defina Illumination dark a partir da calibração da sua câmera, quando houver. É um deslocamento aditivo em contagens brutas; zero é o valor do exemplo.

scenes.narration: Ative Illumination QC e escolha uma regra para modelos ausentes. Com error selecionado, a falta da correção de uma placa interrompe o processamento para que você possa resolver.

scenes.speech_text: Pressione Run e leia no console o caminho do modelo salvo. Esta etapa estima o modelo; ative-o numa análise posterior para aplicar a correção.

scenes.narration: Inspecione o campo de iluminação estimado: ele deve mostrar variação suave de brilho, sem estruturas indesejadas em forma de célula. A correção subtrai o deslocamento de escuro e divide por este campo de média um.

objectives: Escolher as entradas de contagem e as configurações de controle de qualidade.

lessons.title: Hit List: filtrar candidatos e exportar uma lista curta
lessons.description: Carregue resultados do Regression, filtre por valor q, número de guias e concordância e exporte os candidatos selecionados.
objectives: Abrir os resultados de exemplo do Regression com o script complementar fornecido.
Filtrar candidatos e ler os efeitos e a concordância entre guias.
Exportar as linhas selecionadas como CSV, Markdown ou HTML.
lessons.prerequisite: Extraia Hit_List_real_results_companion.zip e ative o seu ambiente do spaCR. O atalho Hits atual do Regression não mostra o painel; execute python hit_list_companion.py e use Browse para ir até a pasta de resultados extraída. O script complementar não se conecta ao Investigate. Use wells_with_gene de results_gene.csv para a contagem de poços de suporte: o n_obs=0 exportado não é o suporte real. O exemplo não contém genes que atendam q <= 0.05.

scenes.narration: Na tela Home, abra Regression e escolha Hits. Se o painel continuar oculto, use o script complementar fornecido com esta aula para abrir o Hit List.
scenes.speech_text: Na tela Home, abra Regression e escolha Hits. Se o painel continuar oculto, use o script complementar fornecido com esta aula para abrir o Hit List.

scenes.narration: O exemplo carrega trezentos e vinte e cinco genes. Alargue as colunas para ler o efeito, P, q e a concordância entre guias. Os efeitos são efeitos marginais padronizados. Para a contagem de poços de suporte, leia wells_with_gene em results_gene.csv; a contagem de observações zero exportada indica que o suporte não está disponível.

lessons.title: Prediction Profiler: explore a fitted model
lessons.description: Load model coefficients, vary one input while holding others fixed, and inspect predicted responses.
objectives: Load coefficients with the correct model link.
Sweep one input and adjust held values.
Inspect response curves and sensitivity.
lessons.prerequisite: Download the synthetic coefficient example, or use coefficients from a suitable fitted model. Match its link and input encoding. The coefficient-file route assumes input ranges of zero to one; separate marginal effects are not substitutes for a jointly fitted prediction model.

scenes.narration: Open Regression, then Prediction Profiler to explore predicted responses from a fitted model. The linked example uses synthetic data.
Download and unzip the example, then Browse to the synthetic OLS coefficients CSV. Include the intercept when supplying your own fitted coefficients.
Set Link to the function used by the fitted model. Keep identity for this ordinary least-squares example.
Check the range information after loading. The coefficient-file route assumes each input spans zero to one. Confirm that this matches your intended use before interpreting the curves.
Select Input A for the sweep. Move the held Input B slider to one and inspect the resulting response curve.
Move B to zero and compare the response values. Watch the axis scale as well as the line, because the plot may rescale.
Click Reset held values to return the sliders to the midpoints of their assumed ranges, one half in this example.
Select Input B in the ranked list to sweep B while holding A fixed. The ranking summarizes model sensitivity over its configured input ranges.
Change Points to choose the number of positions evaluated along the plotted curve. Eleven gives a coarser grid than sixty-one without changing the fitted model.
Adjust the held values to explore further scenarios, then reset when finished. Interpret the curves as model predictions and assess real experimental effects with appropriate data.

lessons.title: AnnData Export: save measured objects and features
lessons.description: Export joined measurements or one object table to h5ad, choose how to handle missing values and retain object metadata.
objectives: Open AnnData Export and select a measured project.
Choose joined or single-table measurements and a missing-value policy.
Export an h5ad file with feature names and object metadata.
lessons.prerequisite: Use a project that has completed Measure, or download the measurements example through Annotate. Work on a copy of the project and retain its source images. Use the current nightly build for the normal exporter shown here.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Measure, then choose AnnData Export. Use this tool to save measured objects, their features and their metadata together in an h5ad file.
Select your measured project as Source. For this walkthrough, use a copy of the measurements example available through Annotate. Keep its measurements folder and source images together.
Leave Single table empty to combine the selected tables onto cell rows. Set an output filename ending in h5ad. Keep float32 and gzip for a compact numerical export.
Set Row limit to zero to include every available row. A positive limit is useful for a small first export. Leave Compute UMAP off when you only need the measurement matrix.

Choose keep as the missing-value policy, then press Run. Read the completion message. The joined example contains two thousand three hundred forty-one cell rows and one thousand one hundred thirty-six features.
Set Single table to cell and choose a new output filename. Run again to export the cell measurements alone. Here, the result has two hundred sixty-one features and twenty-eight missing values.

Choose mean to replace missing feature values with observed column means. The export also records their original positions in a missing-value layer. Use this policy when mean imputation fits your downstream analysis.
Choose drop_features to remove columns containing missing values. This example retains all cells and removes four feature columns. Check the retained feature names when comparing exports.
Choose drop_objects to remove rows containing missing feature values. Seven cells are removed here. Consider whether the excluded objects could change your analysis.
Choose nucleus as the single table when you need one row per nucleus. This example produces two thousand six hundred eighty-two nuclei and three hundred forty-one features.

Enable Register artifact to make the output discoverable in the project. Save each policy under a distinct filename and retain its settings. The h5ad file contains measurements and metadata; keep the source images separately.

Open the resulting h5ad file in your downstream analysis and inspect its shape, feature names and object metadata. From Python, run_anndata_export uses the same settings, while build_anndata constructs the data in memory.

lessons.title: PCA: explore measurements and export components
lessons.description: Load measured objects, choose features, compare principal components and export scores, loadings and explained variance.
objectives: Load a measurement database or CSV and select features.
Choose scaling, missing-value handling and filters.
Inspect component scores and loadings, then export three result tables.
lessons.prerequisite: Download the example from the Annotate tutorial and work with a copy of measurements.db. This walkthrough uses its cell table, with 2,341 measured objects across four wells. Keep the original database and record your feature list, filters, scaling and missing-value policy.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Image UMAP, then choose PCA. Use PCA to summarize several measurement columns as principal components. Start with the measurements database from the linked Annotate example.
Click Load table beside the PCA heading. Open measurements.db and select cell. Check the displayed table and object count. You can also load a CSV containing measurement columns.

Clear the feature search and click None to untick all visible features. Select cell_area, cell_channel_1_mean_intensity and cell_perimeter. Clear the search again, set Components to three, then click Run PCA.

Keep Scale on Standardise to center each feature and divide by its sample standard deviation. Read the scree plot: the first two components explain about sixty-five point seven and thirty-one point seven percent of the selected features’ variance.
Choose rowID in Colour, PC three on X and PC one on Y. These controls redraw the fitted result. Each point represents a cell; rowID identifies a spatial row in this example.

Return to PC one and PC two. Toggle Loadings biplot to show or hide feature arrows. The arrows show correlations with the displayed components; use their directions and the dashed reference circle to compare features.

Choose Centre only to fit using the original measurement scales. The first component now explains about ninety point one percent. Scaling changes the question being summarized. Restore Standardise to compare features on a common scale.

In the right-hand filter, add cell_area and set the minimum to twenty-one thousand nine hundred twenty-five. The panel refits PCA on the remaining one thousand one hundred seventy-one cells, so both the population and component directions change.

Click Clear all in the filter to restore the full population. Check the object count after filtering. The source database stays unchanged; the displayed result is recalculated for the chosen population.

Select cell_channel_0_homogeneity_distance_32 as a fourth feature. Click Run PCA to include it in the result. This example has seven missing measurements in that column; use NaN to choose how the fit handles them.

With Auto, features missing in more than two percent of rows are removed, then incomplete rows are dropped. Here all four features remain and seven cells are excluded. Read the report to see the features and objects actually analyzed.

Choose Drop features to remove any selected feature containing missing values. In this example the texture feature is removed and all cells remain. The result notice shows which features were excluded, even while their checkboxes remain ticked.

Choose Mean-impute to retain all cells and features by replacing missing values with the observed feature mean during calculation. Here seven values are replaced. Record this choice when presenting the result; the replacements are estimates.

Choose Complete cases to retain the selected features and exclude incomplete rows. To return to the original example, choose Auto, untick the texture feature, clear the search, click Run PCA and set Colour to none.

Click Export and choose a base name such as pca_example. The panel writes three CSV files: scores for analyzed objects, loadings and correlations for features, and explained variance for components. The scores table also includes the source measurement columns.

Open the exported tables and keep them with your feature list, filters and analysis settings. Treat the cells as observations within their wells when interpreting separation. For a repeatable Python analysis, use pca and PCASpec from spacr.qt.widgets.pca_model.

lessons.title: Tabulate: summarize measurements by well and field
lessons.description: Group measured objects, select summary statistics, inspect missing groups and export a pivot table or send it to Graph Builder.
objectives: Load measurements and group them by well or field.
Choose values, statistics and filters while checking contributing counts.
Export CSV summaries and refresh their Graph Builder plots.
lessons.prerequisite: Download the measurement example from the Annotate tutorial and work with a copy of measurements.db. Its cell table has 2,341 objects across four wells. Keep spatial labels distinct from treatment labels, and choose the grouping level appropriate to your experiment.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Database Browser, then choose Tabulate. Use this tool to summarize measurement columns by well, field or another group. This walkthrough uses the database from the linked Annotate example.

Inside Tabulate, click Load table, open measurements.db and choose cell. Use Tabulate’s own controls to select its input and export. Check the table and the two thousand three hundred forty-one loaded objects.

Choose Plate slash row slash column to group by plate and well. Leave Values empty to count source rows. The four wells contain six hundred fifteen, five hundred twenty-five, seven hundred and five hundred one cells.

Search for fieldID and drag it into Columns. This creates a well-by-field grid. Hover over a blank cell to inspect it: this example has one combination with no source rows. Keep that distinct from a measured zero.

Clear Columns, then drag cell_area into Values. The default summary shows count, mean and sample standard deviation. Searching finds column names; changing the axes or statistics recomputes the summary.
Hover over a result cell to see all its statistics and the contributing count, including lines hidden by the row height. Standard deviation describes variation among the objects in that group.

Enable median, sem and quantile to add those statistics. Set Quantile at to zero point seven five for the upper quartile. SEM uses the available object count; choose the experimental replicate level separately when estimating biological uncertainty.

Set Quantile at to zero point five to display the median. The first well now shows twenty-two thousand four hundred for both. Restore zero point seven five and switch off the extra statistics to return to the simpler summary.

Replace cell_area with cell_channel_0_homogeneity_distance_32. This feature has seven missing values, so its contributing counts are smaller than the source-row counts. Use those counts when comparing groups.

Restore cell_area and click Export CSV inside Tabulate. Choose a new filename. This well summary contains the three grouping keys, count, mean and standard deviation. Keep your grouping, statistic and filter choices beside the exported file.

Click Plot this table to send the summary to Graph Builder. Drag columnID onto X, mean onto Y and rowID onto Colour. Check the inferred column types: Automatic treats these four distinct means as categories in this example and displays a heatmap.

Add a cell_area filter with a minimum of twenty-one thousand nine hundred twenty-five. The pivot updates immediately for the remaining objects. Click Plot this table again whenever you want to transfer the updated summary to the chart.

After clicking Plot this table, inspect the updated group means. An area-filter note can appear because the transferred summary contains mean rather than cell_area. The object filter has already been applied upstream in Tabulate.
Click Clear all in the filter, then Plot this table again to restore the original well summary. Save filtered and unfiltered exports under different names when you need both.

For a field-level summary, drag fieldID into Rows after the well keys. Each populated row now summarizes one field within a well. Inspect the contributing counts and keep this grouping level consistent when comparing results.

Click Plot this table, put fieldID on X, keep mean on Y and rowID on Colour, then choose Scatter from Plot. In this example mean is now recognized as continuous. Confirm the displayed column types and axis labels.

The scatter plot displays fifty-one field means. Colours identify spatial rows, and repeated field labels can belong to different wells. Use the original object table when you want to select individual cells and inspect their images.

Export the field summary as a separate CSV. It contains fifty-two grid rows, with the empty combination left blank; the chart contains fifty-one populated groups. For Python, use pivot and PivotSpec from spacr.qt.widgets.pivot_spec, then to_csv to save the result.

lessons.title: Feature Dictionary: find definitions and units
lessons.description: Search by measurement name or concept, read the definition and units, and copy useful reference text.
objectives: Find a definition by name or concept.
Narrow the results with concept and object filters.
Read units and notes, then copy the definition.
lessons.prerequisite: Have a measurement column name ready, or start with an idea such as size or intensity. The built-in dictionary can be opened without loading a project.

scenes.narration: Open Help, then Feature Dictionary. Use this window when you want to understand a measurement column in a results table or plot.
Type size in the search field and select Area from the results. The definition appears on the right, and the matching list updates as you type.
Choose a concept and object type to narrow the definitions. Try intensity and cell. Reset the selectors to Any concept and Any object for a broader search.
Search for cell_channel_1_mean_intensity and select Mean intensity. Read the statistic and units to understand what the column describes.
Scroll down to Channel, Module and Computed by for more detail. Use the named computing function as a starting point in the API reference.

Look up cell_area and read Unit. In two-dimensional measurements it represents area; in three-dimensional measurements it represents volume. Check the measurement units recorded in your project before converting values.

Read Note for qualifications such as values already expressed in physical units. For a dictionary of the columns actually present in a database, use describe_database and export_dictionary from Python.
If no definitions match, clear the filters and try a broader term or the exact column name. Custom features may need documentation from the workflow that created them.
Select the definition text and copy it into your notes. Use the Python export functions when you need a project-specific dictionary file, then return to your table or plot.

lessons.title: Small Multiples: compare groups with shared or separate axes
lessons.description: Load measurements, arrange grouped scatter plots, choose axis scales and filters, and add a derived column.
objectives: Load measurements and assign axes and facets.
Choose shared, independent or grouped axis limits.
Inspect filters and displayed groups, then add or remove a derived column.
lessons.prerequisite: Download the measurement example from the Annotate tutorial and work with a copy of measurements.db. This walkthrough uses its cell table, with 2,341 objects across four wells. Small Multiples displays plots; use Tabulate to export grouped CSV summaries.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Graph Builder, then Small Multiples. Use this view to compare the same measurements across groups. This example uses the measurements database available from the linked Annotate tutorial.

Click Load table beside the Small Multiples heading. Open a copy of measurements.db and select cell. Check the table and its two thousand three hundred forty-one objects before assigning plot channels.

Drag cell_area onto X and cell_channel_1_mean_intensity onto Y, then choose Scatter. Put rowID on Facet down and columnID on Facet across. Search helps you find column names; each point represents a measured cell.
Choose shared for both scales so all four panels use matching axis limits. Read the group titles and object counts. In this example the facet labels identify spatial rows and columns.
Choose free for X scale and Y scale to give each panel its own limits. This makes within-group patterns easier to see. Compare tick labels carefully because the ranges now differ between panels.
Choose per row for both scales to share limits between panels on each grid row. Different rows can have different ranges. Use this when comparisons within rows are the priority.
Choose per column to share limits within each grid column. You can set X and Y independently. Restore shared on both axes when you want to compare all four wells on common scales.

In Filter, add cell_area and set its minimum to twenty-one thousand nine hundred twenty-five. The grid updates immediately for the remaining one thousand one hundred seventy-one objects. Check the new panel counts.

Click Clear all in Filter to restore the full population. Use Clear all channels on the left when you want to remove the chart assignments instead. Both operations leave the source database unchanged.

Filter columnID to c two and fieldID to f twenty and f twenty-one. Put fieldID on Facet across and keep rowID on Facet down. The row-five, field-twenty panel has no objects; its empty panel represents a missing group.
Clear the filters and restore columnID on Facet across. Set Wrap at to five. Wrapping applies to a single facet channel, so the current two-way grid stays two by two.
Clear Facet down and put fieldID on Facet across. With Wrap at five, the displayed fields fill rows of up to five panels. Unused slots at the end are hidden.

Read the notice below the grid before comparing groups. This view displays twelve field levels; field twenty-one is omitted from the panels. The loaded-row count includes that field, so check which groups are actually visible.

Turn wrapping off and restore rowID and columnID as the two facets. In Columns, name a derived column area_k and enter cell_area divided by one thousand. Check the preview, then click Add column to compute it for the full table.

Drag area_k onto X to display area in thousands of the original units. The vertical coordinates and groups stay the same. This rescales numbers; physical-area conversion requires the correct image calibration.
Put cell_area back on X. Select area_k in Columns and click Remove to delete the derived column from this view. Keep a record of your variables, facets, filters and scale choices.

Use Tabulate when you need an exported CSV summary. For scripted small-multiple plots, use trellis and TrellisSpec from spacr.qt.widgets.trellis_spec with GraphSpec for the chart channels. Interpret the groups at the appropriate experimental replicate level.

lessons.title: Gate Editor: select populations and save their membership
lessons.description: Draw gates on measurements, save reusable boundaries, explore projections and export object membership to a database.
objectives: Load measurements and draw named gates.
Save and reload gate strategies, figures and membership.
Explore three-dimensional views, clustering and filters.
lessons.prerequisite: Download the Annotate example and make a working copy of measurements.db. Gate Editor uses its 2,341 cell measurements; it has no separate example-download button. Export gates writes membership to the chosen database. Gate names should describe the selected measurements until their biological meaning has been established.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Tools and choose Gate Editor. Adjust the dividers so you can see the plot, gate table and side controls. Use the measurement database from the Annotate example.

Click Load table, open your working copy of measurements.db and choose cell. The example contains two thousand three hundred forty-one objects. Keep a copy because Export gates writes membership to this database.
Choose cell_area for X and cell_channel_1_mean_intensity for Y, then select Rectangle. Each point represents an object. Check the feature names and units before drawing.
Drag across the scatter, release and enter a descriptive gate name. The gate stores boundaries in the two selected measurements.

Read the count and percentage beside the gate name. The illustrated region contains six hundred fifty-five objects. Your mouse positions may give different boundaries; save a strategy to repeat an exact selection.
Untick the gate to hide its overlay, then tick it to show it again. Delete gate removes its definition. The Filter tab separately controls the objects displayed beneath the gates.
Click Save gates to write a JSON strategy. Delete the gate, then choose Load gates and open the saved file. Reuse strategies with matching feature names, units and preprocessing.
The loaded strategy restores the saved boundaries and population. Check the axes, outline and count before continuing with another dataset.
Choose Save graph to save the plotted figure. File formats follow your plotting preferences; this example produces PNG and PDF. Keep the JSON strategy beside the figure.
Choose Export gates to write membership flags to the working database’s filters table. Each flag is associated with the object’s plate, well, field, label and type.
Draw a second gate and give it a new name. New shapes are independent of the selected gate, so the second can include objects outside the first. Save this two-gate strategy under a new filename.
Choose three D and set Z to cell_perimeter. Use the spin-axis buttons to rotate the view. Return to two D to inspect the original area-intensity boundaries.
Use From view to create a named box bounded by the three displayed measurements. Check its population count and save the new strategy separately.
Enable x D to compute principal components from eligible measurements. The axis labels show explained variance for each component. Choose two D or three D separately to control the view.

When turning x D off, select the raw measurement axes again. Save projection details separately: the gate JSON does not retain the fitted projection, and component boundaries may differ between independently fitted datasets.

Open Search and widen its panel. Save and remove temporary gates, choose the two raw features, enable scaling and set twenty minimum neighbours and five Walk steps. Click Run walk and review the confirmation values.
Inspect the resulting outlines and population counts. Here Walk chooses a radius near zero point one six seven and finds two populations. Review which objects lie outside those regions.
Save the Walk strategy, remove its gates and switch Walk off. Try radius zero point five to compare the resulting larger region, then choose the strategy appropriate to your analysis.
Reload the saved two-gate strategy. In Filter, add cell_area with a minimum of twenty-one thousand nine hundred twenty-five. The view now contains one thousand one hundred seventy-one objects.
Click Clear all to restore the full population. Check the active filters and gate definitions before interpreting counts or exporting membership.
To inspect the loaded table directly, open the right-hand console and enter len(df). This example returns two thousand three hundred forty-one rows.
Keep your data, JSON strategy and exported membership together. In Python, use GateSet for definitions, gate_mask_over_table to calculate membership and export_gate to save object flags.

lessons.title: Feature Explorer: compare groups and export a feature ranking
lessons.description: Choose a grouping column, rank measurements by AUC or KS, inspect distributions and export the selected features.
objectives: Load measurements and choose the comparison groups.
Read rankings and distributions, then explore filters and computed columns.
Export the intended number of ranked features.
lessons.prerequisite: Download the Annotate example and open a working copy of its measurements.db. It contains 2,341 cells. This walkthrough compares rowID groups r12 and r5, which identify spatial plate rows. Choose a group column appropriate to your own experiment and account for cells sharing wells when interpreting the comparison.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Classify, then Feature Explorer. Use the measurement database from the Annotate example to compare existing features between groups.
Click Load table, choose measurements.db and select cell. Set Split by to rowID. The example groups are spatial plate rows; check that your grouping column represents the comparison you intend.
Choose AUC under Rank by. Separation is the absolute value of twice AUC minus one. Higher in shows the direction, and min n counts finite measurements in the smaller group.
Set Top to four to inspect four overlaid histograms. Within each feature the groups share bin edges, and bar heights show counts. Read both the distributions and the ranking score.
Click Export ranking to save the displayed top features. With Top set to four, the export contains four feature rows. Increase Top before exporting a longer ranking.
Set Top to five hundred to include all two hundred sixty-one scorable features in this example. The plot shows at most eight distributions, even when the exported ranking is longer.
Switch Rank by to KS to compare the largest gap between cumulative distributions. KS can reveal spread differences missed by AUC. Return to AUC to inspect direction through Higher in.
In Filter, add cell_area and set the minimum to twenty-one thousand nine hundred twenty-five. The population changes to one thousand one hundred seventy-one cells, and the ranking updates.
Click Clear all to restore the full population and ranking. Recheck Split by after changing filters so you know which groups are being compared.
Filtering rowID to r12 removes the second group. In this build, Split by then changes automatically to another column. Check that control whenever a filter removes a group.

Clear the filter and explicitly restore rowID under Split by. Keep Shuffle test off for this example: cells share wells, so unrestricted cell-label shuffles do not represent independent experimental replicates.

Open Columns and name a computed column area_k. Enter cell_area divided by one thousand and click Add column with replacement off. Preview displays the first two thousand rows; adding applies the formula to the whole table.
The computed column joins the ranking. Positive rescaling gives it the same AUC and KS as cell_area. Remove the formula to return to the original features.

Export the ranking after checking the population, Split by and Top. For Python, use rank_features and ExplorerSpec from spacr.qt.widgets.feature_rank. Continue with Graph Builder to plot a selected feature in more detail.

lessons.title: Outliers: flag measurements for inspection
lessons.description: Choose features and a robust rule, inspect object and well results, and export flags with the full input table.
objectives: Load measurements and select the features to scan.
Compare MAD, IQR and log-transformed rules.
Read scoring limitations and export rows, flags and a report.
lessons.prerequisite: Use a working copy of measurements.db from the Annotate example. Flags identify observations for inspection; choose thresholds for your analysis. The example has four wells, fewer than the five needed for the across-well comparison. Keep unscored wells distinct from wells that were scored without flags.

scenes.narration: From Home, open QC, then Outliers. Use the database from the Annotate example to flag unusual measurements for inspection.
Click Load table and choose the cell table. Loading scans the selected continuous features automatically. Review the selected features before interpreting this broad initial result.
With the feature search empty, click None to clear all selections. Search for cell_area, tick that feature and click Scan. Changing the selection requires another scan.
Choose MAD, leave Transform at none and set k to three point five. Click Scan. The rule measures distance from the median using a robust scale and flags twenty-six objects in this example.
Open Wells and read well_scored and the reason column. These four wells are unscored because the comparison needs at least five eligible wells. Flagged share summarizes object flags separately.
Open Report to read the rule, centre and scale. In this build, its general well-count explanation is incorrect for this example; use the specific reason in the Wells table: too few eligible wells.

Lower k to flag smaller departures from the centre. At zero point five, the example has one thousand four hundred seventy-nine flags. The object table displays only five hundred rows, so use the flag count rather than the visible row count.
Choose Export and a new filename. The objects CSV retains all input rows with flags; flagged contains only flagged objects. Wells and report save the well summaries and analysis text.
Choose IQR and set c to one point five, then Scan. This applies fences based on the interquartile range and flags fifty-five objects for raw cell area.
Read the IQR report’s fences. Its displayed centre is the midpoint of the first and third quartiles, although this build labels it median. Use the source data when you need the actual median.
Choose log10 and scan again. The centres, scales and distance rule now apply to log-transformed values. Try MAD at three point five to compare its result with the IQR rule.
Return Transform to none, clear the feature selection and choose cell_channel_0_min_intensity alone. Scan the raw values before trying a logarithmic transform.
Choose log10 and click Scan. This feature contains a zero, so the transform is refused and export is disabled. Read the error: any old rows still visible belong to the previous result.

Restore raw cell_area, MAD and k three point five, then Scan. Increasing Min objects per well to seven hundred makes three wells ineligible. The remaining one still cannot support the five-well comparison.
Restore Min objects per well to twenty. Turn Score wells too off and Scan to obtain object flags only. Turn it back on and scan again to include the well summaries.
Export the restored rule under a separate filename. Keep the report with its twenty-six flagged rows, full object table and four well summaries so you can identify the settings used.

For Python, use detect_outliers and OutlierSpec from spacr.qt.widgets.outlier_model. Continue with Feature Explorer to examine distributions or Annotate to inspect matching images before deciding how to handle flagged objects.

lessons.title: Experiment Design: plan a plate and export its well map
lessons.description: Set conditions and replicates, choose a layout, review warnings and export assignments for acquisition and analysis.
objectives: Enter conditions, replicate counts and control roles.
Choose a plate format, edge policy and reproducible random layout.
Export the exact well assignments for later joins to measurements.
lessons.prerequisite: Prepare your condition names, control roles and intended well counts before acquisition. The example requests six negative-control wells, six positive-control wells and twelve treatment wells; choose replication for your own experiment. Keep the plate identifier consistent with later images and measurements.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Data and choose Experiment Design. Start by entering the conditions and controls you want to place on the plate.
Name the plate using the identifier you will use during acquisition. Review Condition, Replicates and Role in the table. Double-click a column boundary to widen it when needed.

Choose a plate format with enough wells for the requested replicates. Selecting six wells for this twenty-four-well plan displays a capacity error. Change the format or the requested counts to continue.
Select ninety-six wells to restore the layout. Use Add condition and Remove selected to edit condition rows, then check the updated plate map.
To edit a replicate count, select its cell and press F two. A single negative-control well triggers a warning. Choose independent experimental replication appropriate to your analysis.
Choose Block layout to group conditions together. Read the positional warnings and inspect the map for potential confounding between condition and position.
Choose Random layout, enable Leave edge empty and set Seed to forty-two. This ninety-six-well plate has sixty interior wells available, with twenty-four assigned by the example plan.
Change Seed to forty-three to generate another arrangement with the same condition counts. Review the placement of controls and treatments across the plate.
Restore Seed forty-two to recover the previous arrangement. Save the seed together with the format, edge policy and condition table.
Drag across wells B zero two to C zero four to select them. This selects wells for inspection; use the condition table and layout controls to change assignments.
Click Export plate map and choose a folder. Keep plate_map.csv, plate_map.json and plate_map_settings.json together.
Open the CSV to inspect one row per assigned well. Join it to later measurements using plateID, rowID and columnID together. The JSON retains the design and its warnings.

For this randomized layout, the settings file reports expressible as false. Use the exact CSV well map for condition labels: whole-row or whole-column treatment settings cannot represent these mixed assignments.

Review the final map before acquisition and retain it with the experiment. In Python, use Condition and PlateDesign, followed by assign_wells, check_design and write_design from spacr.qt.widgets.plate_layout.

lessons.title: Power & Design: explore simulated detection curves
lessons.description: Set library and design assumptions, run simulations and inspect detection fractions, failed fits and caveats.
objectives: Set the library, scoring unit and design assumptions.
Run cell-count and well-count scans with recorded settings.
Read detection fractions and caveats before interpreting a design.
lessons.prerequisite: Prepare assumptions for library size, guides per gene, background, effect and prevalence. This module simulates data. The linked example uses only two replicates per point to show the controls; use enough repetitions and appropriate assumptions for planning. In this build, inspect the table rather than relying on a headline that can recommend the unchanged baseline well count.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Power & Design. Start with the assumptions you want to explore, then use simulated detection curves to compare the displayed cell-count and well-count choices.
Set library size and guides per gene, then choose the scoring unit. With forty genes and four guides per gene, guide scoring uses one hundred sixty units; gene scoring pools guide information.
Review the plate, background, effect and prevalence controls together. The positive-call rate is an assumed classification probability. Choose values that describe your planned analysis.
If an effect below one disables Run, read the unsupported-direction warning. Restore a supported value to continue; this simulator does not cover every possible effect direction.

Set repetitions, seed, backend and the detection threshold. The threshold uses area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. The example uses two replicates per point for a short run; choose more repetitions when estimating detection probability.
Click Run and follow the progress. The simulator scans cell counts and well counts separately. Keep the settings with the completed results.
Read detection counts alongside their denominators. Failed or nonconverged fits remain as non-detections. With two requested replicates, one hundred percent means only two detections out of two.

Use the results table to inspect detection fractions, mean performance among usable fits and nonconvergence. Unavailable mean values are missing results. Interpret average precision relative to the assumed prevalence.

Compare the requested design values directly. This build can recommend increasing to the same baseline well count because the two scans use different random draws. Disregard that headline and use the table and uncertainty to assess the comparison.
Expand the caveats and inspect failed fits or clipped probabilities. Adjust assumptions when they produce outcomes inconsistent with the experiment you intend to model.

Keep the settings and replicate results together. The linked archive contains the example run for inspection. For programmatic output, use the design adapter and simulation APIs; assess assumptions and uncertainty before choosing an experimental design.

lessons.title: Dose Response: fit concentration curves and read their intervals
lessons.description: Load a concentration table, group series, fit logistic curves and keep estimates, intervals and fit warnings together.
objectives: Load the synthetic example and choose concentration, response and grouping columns.
Fit curves and compare profile-likelihood and Wald intervals.
Read unbounded or refused results and save the report.
lessons.prerequisite: Download the linked synthetic dose-response CSV. It contains four illustrative series, nine positive concentrations and a zero-dose vehicle, with three observations per concentration. Supply raw concentration values and prepare any normalization or unit conversion before loading your own data.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Data and choose Dose Response. Prepare a table with explicit concentration and response columns for each series you want to fit.
Download the linked synthetic CSV, then click Load table and open it. The named synthetic series illustrate the controls and different fit outcomes.
The table has one hundred twenty rows across four series. Each includes nine positive concentrations, a zero-dose vehicle and three observations at each concentration.
Set the concentration column to concentration, the response column to response and One curve per to series. Use raw concentrations rather than their logarithms.
Enter the concentration unit in Unit. For this example use micromolar. This field labels the values; convert the numbers upstream if you need a different unit.
Choose Profile likelihood, leave Fit non-monotone data off and click Fit. Inspect the curve panel and results table together, including series with warnings or unavailable estimates.
Select synthetic inhibition. Its midpoint is one point five and its Hill slope is negative. Half-maximum lies halfway between the fitted plateaus, which are five and ninety-five here.
Select synthetic activation. Its midpoint is two and its Hill slope is positive. The selected curve is emphasized, and the report below follows the selected row.

Select the beyond-range example. Its tested concentrations end at one hundred, leaving the midpoint unsupported. Read the reported bound; blank midpoint and interval cells indicate an unavailable estimate.
Select the reversing series and read why the fit is refused. Inspect the response shape and experimental context before deciding whether a monotonic logistic model is appropriate.

Return to inhibition and read the observation counts. Twenty-seven positive-dose observations enter the fit. Three zero-dose controls are summarized separately because zero cannot enter the logarithmic fit.

Read residual error and lack of fit alongside R squared. Keep the replicate structure of your experiment in mind when interpreting uncertainty; repeated rows alone do not establish independent experiments.
Choose Wald and click Fit again to compare interval methods. Changing the selector requires another fit. The interval is calculated on the log midpoint and transformed back to concentration.
Compare the interval endpoints for the well-bracketed series. The midpoint estimates stay similar here; the beyond-range example still has no supported midpoint estimate.
Restore Profile likelihood and click Fit. Check the selected method and corresponding report before copying results.
Sort the table only after completing the fitting comparisons. This build can misalign rows if you refit a sorted table. Select inhibition and confirm that the report names the same series.
Select the report text and copy it with the normal keyboard shortcut. Save the warnings, interval method and input concentrations alongside the result.

For tabular output, use fit_frame and the dose-response result table in Python. This screen has no export button. Retain unbounded and refused rows in your output so every input series stays accounted for.

lessons.title: Explain CV Model: compare predictions with measured features
lessons.description: Load matching predictions and measurements, fit a surrogate and read fidelity before using feature explanations.
objectives: Match the measurement database to saved classifier predictions.
Choose prediction columns, a backend and held-out groups.
Read fidelity, confusion and saved feature summaries.
lessons.prerequisite: Use measurements.db and the predictions CSV from the same Annotate/Classify example objects. Select the saved model class calls as the target. This example has limited surrogate fidelity, so its feature attributions should not be used to explain the vision model. Evaluate the original classifier separately with independent data.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Classify, then choose Explain CV Model at the upper right. Prepare the measurement database and saved predictions for the same cropped objects.
Select measurements.db and the matching predictions CSV. Check the filenames and object identities before continuing. This example uses two hundred thirty-four saved predictions.

Confirm the prediction path with Enter if the column choices have not refreshed. Choose filename for the crop path and predicted_label for the model’s class calls. Select Random Forest, grouping by well and a new output folder.
Click Explain model. The surrogate uses measured features to reproduce the saved class calls. Choose the backend and grouping on this form; use the Python API for additional fitting options.

Read Fidelity first. Here eighty-nine rows have complete features, with sixty-eight used for fitting and twenty-one from another well held out. Compare agreement with the baseline and inspect which rows were excluded.

Open Importance. In this example the fidelity gate withholds the ranking. Review the excluded feature names as well: a name-based leakage warning needs to be checked against what the measurement actually contains.

Open Confusion to compare surrogate calls with the vision model’s calls. Here every held-out object is assigned class one, giving seventeen agreements and four differences. Check performance across classes rather than relying only on overall agreement.
Per-cell SHAP describes the fitted surrogate. When fidelity is inadequate, these values cannot explain the vision model reliably. Keep that limitation with any exported attribution table.
Open Correlations and Feature distributions to inspect the measurements. These GUI tables show up to one thousand rows. Use their saved CSV files to inspect the full summaries.

Open Held-out cells to see object identities and both predictions. Keep the output files, settings and fidelity report together. Continue with the Evaluation tutorial when you need to assess the original classifier.

lessons.title: Investigate Hit: rastrear um gene de Regression até as células medidas
lessons.description: Envie um gene da Hit List para o Investigate Hit, adicione o banco de dados de medições, as predições por célula e as frações de guias e leia as evidências no nível do poço.
objectives: Abrir uma execução de Regression na Hit List, conferir os valores q e enviar um gene para o Investigate Hit.
Escolher o banco de dados de medições, as predições por célula, as frações de guias e a coluna de pontuação.
Ler as abas de evidências, poços, guias e limiar e encontrar as tabelas salvas.
lessons.prerequisite: Extraia Investigate_Hit_real_screen_example.zip. Todo o conteúdo vem de uma mesma triagem real: a execução de Regression com os dados de teste de Regression (as configurações do tutorial de Regression), as predições CV por célula correspondentes e um banco de dados de medições com as medidas reais de forma, tamanho e intensidade dessas mesmas células. Para manter o download pequeno, o banco de dados tem 52 poços: todos os poços analisados com uma guia para o gene 225160 e, para cada um, três poços sem ela da mesma placa. Nenhum gene desta execução rápida de Regression atende a q ≤ 0,05. Trate a investigação como um exemplo prático, e não como um hit confirmado.

scenes.narration: Na tela Home, abra Regression. O Investigate Hit parte de uma execução de Regression concluída. Ele pergunta se as células medidas nos poços ligados a um gene parecem diferentes das células de poços sem esse gene.

lessons.title: Volcano Explorer: inspect results and save a figure
lessons.description: Load Regression results, choose plotted values and reference lines, then save a reusable style and export the figure.
objectives: Open a results family and inspect guide identities and support.
Choose adjusted values, display transforms and reference lines.
Save the style and export PDF or PNG figures.
lessons.prerequisite: Extract Volcano_real_guide_family.zip and use its results folder. It contains 434 guide results from the Regression example. No guide passes the original adjusted-P threshold of 0.05. Effects are standardized marginal effects. Keep the original result table and statistical thresholds with the figure.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Regression, then Volcano Explorer. Extract the linked example archive before choosing the result tables you want to plot.
Click Open results and select the extracted results folder. Each point represents a guide in this family of four hundred thirty-four tests. Keep different correction families separate.
Click Save style to save the opening figure settings, then Load style and select that file. This gives you a saved starting point with matching controls before you edit the figure.
Check alpha at zero point zero five, multiplier at three and the negative-log transform enabled. Read the axis labels: this example plots standardized marginal effects.
Click a point to inspect its source row. Read the guide identifier, raw P, adjusted P and supporting well count together. The selected example has adjusted P around zero point three nine.
Choose the raw permutation-P column to inspect it, then restore adjusted_p_value. Changing the plotted column keeps the underlying analysis and its saved significance flags unchanged.
Toggle negative log ten to compare transformed and original P values. With the transform enabled, smaller P values appear higher. Restore the transformed adjusted-P view for this figure.

Move alpha to zero point five to see how it moves the horizontal reference line, then restore zero point zero five. Editing this line does not recompute statistical tests or their saved significance flags.
Set an explicit effect cutoff of zero point one with multiplier three. The vertical lines appear at minus and plus zero point three. Restore Auto to return to the opening effect-line choice.
Choose wells_with_guide for colour to inspect support across the plotted guides. Restore the significance colours before the final export if you want the original presentation.
Set figure size, font sizes and resolution. This example uses seven by five inches at one hundred fifty dots per inch. Inspect readability; tight cropping can change the saved outer dimensions.
Save the final style as JSON. Change the marker size, then Load style to restore the saved appearance. Keep the style file beside the result table.

Export PDF and PNG, then open the files to check labels, contrast and cropping. Keep the output with the input results and style. In Python, use VolcanoStyle and render_volcano for the same rendering workflow.

lessons.title: Parameter Sweep: compare saved Regression trials
lessons.description: Specify paired inputs and trial settings, run a small sweep, then inspect each trial’s settings, figures and inference checks.
objectives: Select paired score/count files and a sweep output folder.
Choose variable and fixed settings, estimate the trial count and run.
Inspect saved trials and their inference quality before comparison.
lessons.prerequisite: Download the four plate score/count pairs from the Regression tutorial. Use matching plate order and a new output folder. The two illustrated ridge trials complete but fail their inference quality checks; keep computational status separate from statistical suitability.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Regression, then Parameter sweep at the bottom right. Use the four example score and count pairs from the Regression tutorial.

Add the four score files and four count files to the sweep’s own lists, in matching plate order. Check these lists even when the parent Regression form already contains inputs. Choose a new output folder.
Tick alpha and enter zero point zero one and zero point one. Unticked settings stay fixed. Set ridge, parametric inference, well-level mean aggregation and no transform explicitly for this example.
Choose Grid sampling, Maximum trials two and one worker, then click Estimate. Check the number of combinations and resource limits before running. Treat the time estimate as approximate.
Click Start sweep. Each trial writes to its own folder. With one worker, the two trials run in sequence; choose worker counts that fit your available resources.

Inspect the completed rows, then open sweep_results.csv and each trial’s settings and quality-control files. Both illustrated trials finish computation but fail inference checks, so an ok execution status alone is insufficient for selecting a model.
Select the first row and click Show figures for selected row. Inspect the guide results and axis labels. The plot omits the intercept from the coefficient table.
Switch Level to Gene to inspect the gene family separately. Check its rows, effects and quality-control results before comparing it with the guide view.
Switch back to Guide. Read sample support from the input and diagnostic files: the example’s rows-fitted summary counts output coefficient rows rather than wells.
Keep each trial’s settings, summary and quality-control files with its figures. Use Regression Diagnostics for further inspection, or SweepSpace and run_sweep from Python for a scripted comparison.

lessons.title: Import Images: map image identities and create a project
lessons.description: Scan image names and metadata, review the proposed well/field/channel mapping, save a plan and import copies into a project.
objectives: Scan microscope images and resolve naming questions.
Choose a destination, plate name and copy or link behavior.
Save a reusable plan and import images for Mask.
lessons.prerequisite: Download the Mask example first. This walkthrough uses copies of fields E01/F001 and L01/F009, with four channels each. Its prepared copies omit the redundant A token immediately before Z while preserving well, field and channel identities. Keep the originals and use acquisition records when resolving unfamiliar tokens.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Data, choose Import, then Import Images. Start with the microscope image files you want to organize into a project.
Use the Mask example for this walkthrough. Select copies of one field from each of two wells, with four channels per field. Keep the original download unchanged.
Click Scan. If it asks what a filename token means, check the acquisition records before assigning it. Continue only when the proposed identities distinguish the fields and channels unambiguously.

Scan the prepared example copies. Their redundant acquisition token has been removed, while the well, field and channel tokens remain. Check that the proposal lists eight images, two wells, two field numbers and four channels.
Compare the proposal with the filenames. Enable Read inside each file when you need embedded axis metadata. Set Sample large enough to inspect the files you intend to import.

Choose a destination outside the input folder and enter the plate name. Turn Link instead of copy off for independent copies. Links save disk space but require the original files to remain accessible.

For tiled acquisitions, choose whether to stitch, retain separate tiles or skip them. Review the resulting field organization before measuring. These example images are separate fields, so they do not need stitching.
Click Save plan to retain the source and mapping choices as JSON. Keep the plan with the acquisition notes and original images.
Click Load plan to reload the source and saved answers. Review the new proposal before importing, especially when the source files have changed.
Click Import and read the summary. This example produces eight image copies with no skipped files. Open the resulting project in Mask and inspect Live preview before starting segmentation.

lessons.title: Regression Diagnostics: inspect the saved analysis reports
lessons.description: Open a completed run’s design and inference reports, inspect support and dependencies, and use the findings when choosing the next analysis.
objectives: Open the diagnostic folder for the intended Regression run.
Read design support, identifiability and inference summaries.
Keep diagnostics with their settings and rerun after changing an analysis.
lessons.prerequisite: Complete the Regression example using its four score/count pairs. The illustrated permutation run uses 199 permutations and a minimum of two wells. Keep its settings and result families together when interpreting the diagnostic panels.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Regression. After an analysis completes, click Diagnostics. Check the folder path: this shortcut opens the newest diagnostics folder it finds in the project.

Read the diagnostic files in that folder in order: design identifiability, then design diagnostics with the collinear guide pairs, then inference diagnostics, and last the summary that pulls them together.

Start with Design identifiability. Compare the number of wells, parameters and the design rank. This example has more parameters than its rank supports, so it cannot identify a unique simultaneous coefficient for every guide.
Inspect guide support across wells. The example includes many guides found in only one well. Distinguish the full design from the filtered family of guides actually tested.
Open Design diagnostics and the collinear-pairs table. Identify predictors that always occur together or have weak support before attributing their effects separately.
Open Inference diagnostics. Inspect the P-value distribution, null comparison and discoveries across adjusted thresholds. This example has no discoveries at the displayed threshold.

Check the number of permutations when interpreting P values. With one hundred ninety-nine permutations, the smallest attainable empirical P value is zero point zero zero five. Plan the resolution needed for your multiple-testing correction.
A permutation analysis does not produce fitted residuals from a simultaneous regression model. Look for residual panels when using a mode that supplies observed and fitted values.
Read the summary alongside the individual panels. Its overall assessment reflects the worst panel assessment, so open the corresponding report to understand the reason.

Return to Regression to revise inputs or analysis settings deliberately. Run the revised analysis and inspect its new diagnostics. Keep earlier output folders separate so each report remains associated with its settings.

lessons.title: Embeddings: load crops and compare channel policies
lessons.description: Load image crops from Home, choose the encoder and channel policy, run Embed and inspect the feature preview.
objectives: Load a crop folder through the Embeddings screen.
Choose the backbone, batch size and channel policy.
Inspect the vector preview and save full results through the supplied Python helper.
lessons.prerequisite: Install spaCR with its embeddings extra. Download the Annotate example and locate plate1/data/single_nucleus/uninfected/plate1_E02/cell_png. For the small example shown here, copy the first sixteen PNGs in sorted filename order into a new folder. The first encoder run downloads pretrained weights if they are not cached. The optional Embeddings_API_example.zip provides a helper for saving complete matrices.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Embeddings in Data. You will load image crops, choose how their channels are encoded and generate one numerical feature vector per object.

Choose crop folder under Crops from. You can also use a measurements database when you want to select an object class, plate or condition. This walkthrough uses the crop folder from Annotate’s downloadable example.
Copy sixteen example PNGs into a working folder. Enter that folder’s path and press Enter, or use Browse. Set At most to sixteen, then click Load crops.

Read the loaded crop count, size and channel count. The example contains sixteen images, each two hundred twenty-four pixels square with three stored channels. Check the crop export’s channel mapping before comparing results.
Choose Per channel to encode each channel separately and concatenate its features. Keep resnet18 as the Backbone and set Batch to four for this small run. Smaller batches reduce memory use.

Click Embed and wait for the preview. The example produces sixteen object vectors with one thousand five hundred thirty-six dimensions. The table shows only the first few dimensions and, for larger runs, up to fifty objects.
Select Project to three and click Embed again. This encodes the combined image instead of each channel separately. Use the same crops and backbone when comparing the two policies.

The projected example has five hundred twelve dimensions per object. Keep the channel policy and encoder settings with your results. Use the complete vectors for downstream analysis; individual dimensions are not biological measurements.

The screen currently provides a preview without an export button. To save complete matrices, download the linked Python helper and follow its README. It writes vectors, object filenames, settings and exploratory plots to a new output folder.

lessons.title: OPS: from sequencing images to cell barcodes
lessons.description: Load the OPS test data, choose the image and decoding settings, run the analysis and find the barcode assignments in the output database.
objectives: Open OPS inside Mask and load its example images and barcode library.
Choose the input and output folders and understand the main alignment and decoding settings.
Run OPS and inspect nucleus barcode assignments in the output database.
lessons.prerequisite: Open spaCR. Use Load test data inside OPS for the example sequencing images and guide library. For your own experiment, prepare sequencing-cycle TIFFs with their acquisition filenames and a matching barcode-library CSV.

scenes.narration: From Home, open Mask, then turn on OPS. This page takes sequencing-cycle images and assigns decoded barcodes to nuclei.

Click Load test data. The example includes two image sites across eleven sequencing cycles and a matching barcode library. When loading finishes, spaCR fills the input, library, plate and output fields.
In OPS input, check the sequencing image folder and the barcode-library CSV. Choose a destination for the results. The example writes to the ops_output folder inside its downloaded project.
Leave the phenotype image folder empty for this example. When you have a matching phenotype acquisition, select its folder here to record how its fields align with the sequencing images.

Under OPS alignment, choose the nucleus segmentation model. Diameter sets the expected nucleus size in pixels. Raster overlap describes the overlap between neighboring acquired tiles; use the value from your acquisition. Keep the example settings for this first run.

Window overlap controls how much neighboring segmentation windows share. It should be larger than the largest nucleus so objects at window edges can be included whole. Increasing it adds processing time.
Under OPS decoding, set the four base channels in G, T, A, C order. The example uses CY3, A594, CY5 and CY7. For your own images, match these names to the channel names in the TIFF filenames.

Read threshold controls how bright a spot must be to count as a read. Raising it selects stronger spots; lowering it includes fainter spots and more background. Footprint controls how far beyond a nucleus a read can lie and still contribute to its barcode.
Turn on Store reads if you want to inspect the individual read calls later. This saves an additional table and uses more disk space. Leave it off for a compact first run.
Check OPS performance, then press Run. GPU enables acceleration where available. Workers controls how many fields are decoded at once; lower it if memory is limited. Follow the progress in Console.

When Console shows Finished, open Help, then Database Browser, and choose measurements.db in the selected output folder. Beside it, each well has a folder, here A1, holding its OPS report with the decoding summary and any warnings.

The ops_barcodes table gives each nucleus its barcode, read support and matched guide; ops_objects holds the same nucleus identifiers with their image coordinates. Those identifiers are the bridge to the rest of your screen: join the barcodes to your phenotype measurements through them, then aggregate for Regression. Keep the database, reports and settings together.

lessons.title: spaCR screens
lessons.description: Acompanhe uma triagem agrupada baseada em imagens desde a tela Home, passando pelas medições de imagens, pela classificação de fenótipos e pelas contagens de códigos de barras, até a regressão.
objectives: Escolha um módulo inicial a partir dos dados que você já tem.
Identifique o que cada módulo lê e grava.
Siga as lições dos módulos e os contratos da API vinculados para a próxima etapa.
lessons.prerequisite: Instale o spaCR e abra a tela Home. Escolha os dados iniciais do seu fluxo de trabalho e siga as lições de módulos vinculadas para ver os controles e os dados de exemplo.

scenes.narration: Uma triagem agrupada conta sua história duas vezes, uma em imagens e outra em leituras de sequenciamento, e o spaCR junta as duas no fim. No lado das imagens, Mask e Measure transformam seus campos de microscópio em células medidas, e Annotate e Classify transformam essas células em pontuações de fenótipo. No lado do sequenciamento, Map Barcodes transforma leituras em contagens de guias. O Regression junta os dois por placa e poço. Entre onde seus resultados começam.
scenes.speech_text: Uma triagem agrupada conta sua história duas vezes, uma em imagens e outra em leituras de sequenciamento, e o espáquer junta as duas no fim. No lado das imagens, Mask e Measure transformam seus campos de microscópio em células medidas, e Annotate e Classify transformam essas células em pontuações de fenótipo. No lado do sequenciamento, Map Barcodes transforma leituras em contagens de guias. O Regression junta os dois por placa e poço. Entre onde seus resultados começam.

scenes.narration: Tudo começa com suas imagens de microscópio. Abra Mask em Home, escolha os canais e um modelo de segmentação e confira a pré-visualização antes de executar. O Mask encontra os objetos em cada campo e salva cada campo como uma matriz combinada, com os canais de imagem empilhados junto com as máscaras de rótulos. Essas matrizes combinadas são o que o Measure abre em seguida. O pequeno banco de contagens que o Mask deixa é só uma contagem, ainda não uma tabela de características.

scenes.narration: Em seguida, abra Measure em Home e aponte-o para o mesmo projeto, com os índices de canal de imagem e de máscara definidos corretamente. O Measure lê cada matriz combinada, imagens e planos de rótulos juntos, e grava cada célula, núcleo ou parasita como uma linha em measurements.db. Ative o salvamento de recortes e ele também corta um pequeno PNG em volta de cada objeto, indexado em png_list. Daqui a história se divide. O Annotate mostra esses recortes para você rotular exemplos, e o Classify aprende com os recortes ou com as características medidas, então mantenha estáveis as identidades dos objetos.

scenes.narration: Antes que um classificador aprenda qualquer coisa, ele precisa de exemplos. Abra Annotate em Home e ele mostra os recortes de objetos que o Measure salvou ou transmite. Percorra células representativas e rotule-as. Cada rótulo é gravado em uma coluna de anotação da tabela png_list, ligado à identidade daquele objeto. Use uma coluna separada para cada pergunta e reserve alguns objetos rotulados para a avaliação. Essa coluna de anotação é a que o Classify usa para treinar em seguida.

scenes.narration: Abra Classify em Home, e aqui seus rótulos viram pontuações. O Classify tem duas famílias, e seus dados escolhem entre elas. Computer Vision aprende com os próprios recortes de objetos, enquanto Tabular Machine Learning aprende com as colunas de características medidas. De qualquer forma, ele treina com os rótulos que você criou no Annotate, se avalia nos objetos que você reservou e salva o modelo treinado, um pacote de avaliação e as pontuações, como arquivos CSV e, quando combinadas, em png_list. Escolha a coluna de pontuação CV ou ML que você pretende testar, mantenha intacta a identidade de placa e poço e leve-a para o Regression.

scenes.narration: Enquanto as imagens seguem por um caminho, as leituras de sequenciamento seguem por outro. Abra Map Barcodes em Home, entregue a ele seus arquivos FASTQ e as referências de códigos de barras que codificam sua triagem, e ele conta quais guias apareceram em cada poço. Confira as contagens mapeadas e o QC dos códigos de barras antes de confiar nelas. O unique_combinations.csv que ele grava é a tabela de contagens de guias que o Regression associa às suas pontuações de fenótipo, poço a poço.

scenes.narration: É aqui que as duas metades da triagem se encontram. Abra Regression em Home e entregue a ele as duas coisas: as pontuações de fenótipo do Classify e as contagens de guias do Map Barcodes. O Regression as associa por placa e poço, então essas chaves precisam coincidir nos dois arquivos. Escolha a coluna de resposta e seus controles, execute o ajuste e abra os diagnósticos antes de acreditar em qualquer hit. Se seus códigos de barras foram lidos opticamente com o OPS, primeiro junte e agregue os objetos decodificados aos seus dados de fenótipo e de guias; o OPS não entrega uma tabela de contagens pronta. O Regression também pode modelar uma resposta medida diretamente. Ele grava uma pasta de resultados com coeficientes, tabelas de hits, configurações e figuras de diagnóstico.

scenes.narration: Assim, uma triagem agrupada corre como dois fluxos que se encontram em Regression. Antes de abri-lo, confira se os identificadores de placa e poço batem entre suas pontuações, suas contagens de guias e seu layout de placa, e mantenha com a execução a coluna de anotação, as configurações do classificador e as referências de códigos de barras. As lições de módulos vinculadas percorrem cada etapa; você também pode escolher o passo a passo da triagem agrupada em Home.

lessons.title: Entradas e saídas dos módulos
lessons.description: Encontre os dados de entrada, as saídas salvas, os produtores anteriores e os consumidores posteriores de cada módulo atual, incluindo ferramentas internas de um módulo de Home.
objectives: Escolha um módulo inicial a partir dos dados que você já tem.
Identifique o que cada módulo lê e grava.
Siga as lições dos módulos e os contratos da API vinculados para a próxima etapa.
lessons.prerequisite: Instale o spaCR e abra a tela Home. Escolha os dados iniciais do seu fluxo de trabalho e siga as lições de módulos vinculadas para ver os controles e os dados de exemplo.

scenes.narration: Pense nesta lição como um mapa de para onde vai cada arquivo. Cada capítulo é um módulo: como abri-lo, o que ele lê, o que grava e qual módulo recebe essa saída em seguida. Comece pelos arquivos que você tem ou pelo resultado de que precisa e siga as passagens a partir daí. Mantenha os identificadores de objeto, placa e poço junto com os dados durante todo o percurso.
